title: Conduct a range of livestock health care practices in extensive farming conditions

lessons.title: Health care on extensive farms: what is different
lessons.html:
Health care on extensive farms: what is different

This work experience module is done on a real extensive farm, where cattle, sheep or goats graze large camps of veld. You will take part in the farm's health care work under supervision and build a record of what you did.

The challenges

  • Distance: animals may be kilometres from the homestead and only seen every few days. Problems can go unnoticed.
  • Handling: animals are less used to people, so gathering and working them takes planning and skill.
  • Facilities: kraals and crushes may be far apart; mobile equipment is often used.
  • Environment: ticks, poisonous plants, predators, heat, drought and floods all affect health.
  • Vet access: the nearest vet may be far away, so the team must recognise problems early and give first-line treatment as the vet has instructed.

Planning gathering days

Combine tasks to reduce the number of times animals are gathered: for example, vaccinate, dose, tick-treat, condition score and count in one session, as the health plan allows. Plan gathering in the cool of the morning. Make sure water is available in the kraal. Use quiet, experienced riders or walkers and avoid running animals, especially heavily pregnant females.

Regular camp inspections

On each camp visit, check the animals from a distance and then closer, count them, inspect water and lick, and look for sick or dead animals, poisonous plants after rain or fire, and signs of predators. Use binoculars where animals are wild. Record on a field sheet or phone app: date, camp, count, observations.

Your logbook

Record each health task you take part in: date, animals, task, product, your role and your supervisor's signature. This is evidence for your work experience assessment.

lessons.title: Carrying out the health programme in the field
lessons.html:
Carrying out the health programme in the field

Vaccination and dosing

Follow the farm's health plan and the product labels. In the kraal, set up a clean work table out of the sun for the cooler box, syringes and dosing guns. Calibrate dosing guns and check syringes before starting. Work steadily through the group, marking each animal as treated. Change needles regularly. Record product, batch, dose and number of animals treated.

Tick control

On extensive farms ticks are controlled by plunge dips, spray races or pour-ons. Strategic tick control aims to protect animals at the times of highest tick activity while allowing some exposure where the vet advises, so that animals keep their natural resistance to tick-borne diseases. Follow the farm's strategy and the label. Check dip strength and tank level as required.

Worm control

Many farms use targeted selective treatment for sheep and goats: only animals that need it are dosed, using FAMACHA scores, body condition or faecal egg counts. This saves money and slows resistance. Record each animal's score and treatment.

Dealing with sick animals in the veld

  1. Assess the animal from a safe distance.
  2. If it can walk, bring it to a kraal or sick camp quietly.
  3. Examine it and take its temperature.
  4. Report to the supervisor; give treatment only as instructed.
  5. Record the case and check the animal daily.

Dead animals

Record the tag and location. Do not open carcasses of animals that died suddenly or bled from body openings - anthrax is possible. Report to your supervisor; suspected controlled diseases go to the state vet. Dispose of carcasses as directed, away from water sources.

Safety

Wear PPE for chemicals and afterbirths, work in pairs with cattle, and never stand in a crush with an animal.

lessons.title: Poisonous plants, predators and reflecting on practice
lessons.html:
Poisonous plants, predators and reflecting on practice

Plant poisoning

South Africa has many poisonous plants, such as tulp, slangkop, gifblaar and others that vary by region. Poisoning risk is often highest when animals are hungry, when they are moved into a new camp, after fire, or when the first green growth appears after rain. Learn the dangerous plants on your farm with your supervisor. Signs vary but may include sudden deaths, bloat, staggering, trembling or diarrhoea. Move animals out of the camp, call the supervisor and the vet, and do not try home remedies without advice.

Predators

Jackals and caracal cause big losses of lambs and kids. Losses must be recorded with location and evidence. Methods such as kraaling at night, guard dogs, alpacas or donkeys, collars and shepherding can help. Any lethal predator control must follow provincial conservation rules; do not set poison or traps on your own.

Welfare on extensive farms

Even far from the homestead, animals must have water, feed, protection from extreme weather and prompt care when ill or injured, as the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 requires. Animals that cannot be treated should be humanely euthanised by a vet or trained person, not left to suffer.

Reflecting on your work

At the end of each week of work experience, write a short reflection:

  • What health tasks did I do?
  • What went well?
  • What problems did I see, and how were they handled?
  • What did I learn from the vet or supervisor?
  • What do I still need to practise?

Ask your supervisor to sign the logbook and give feedback. Over time this shows your growing competence across vaccination, dosing, tick control, examination, wound care and record keeping.

Key points

  • Distance means problems can go unnoticed; inspect camps deliberately.
  • Combine health tasks on gathering days and handle animals calmly.
  • Use targeted worm treatment and follow the tick control strategy.
  • Do not open sudden-death carcasses; report them.
  • Keep a signed logbook of every task as evidence.

quiz.question: Why are health tasks often combined on one gathering day?

options.text: To reduce the number of times animals are gathered and stressed
Because remedies expire the same day

quiz.question: When is the risk of plant poisoning often highest?

options.text: When animals are hungry, moved to a new camp or after fire

quiz.question: What is targeted selective treatment for worms?

options.text: Dosing only animals that need it, based on scores or egg counts

quiz.question: Which is a correct response to predator losses?

options.text: Set poison in the veld yourself
Shoot any wild animal you see
Record losses and use methods like kraaling or guard animals within the rules
